extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students studying real analysis / metric topology
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and convergence tests concerning compactness in metric spaces and numerical sequences/series in R (including subsequences, Cauchy sequences, lim sup/inf, and standard series convergence tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open cover / subcover / finite subcover
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of open sets {U_α | α ∈ Λ} is an open cover of S ⊂ X if S ⊂ ⋃_{α∈Λ} U_α. For Λ' ⊂ Λ, if {U_α | α ∈ Λ'} also covers S then it is a subcover; if Λ' is finite it is a finite subcover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: U_n = (n, n+1.5) (n∈Z) is an open cover of R; no finite subcollection covers R. Use these notions when defining compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded subset (metric space)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset S of (X,d) is bounded if there exist C>0 and x0∈X such that d(x,x0) < C for every x∈S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to characterize compactness in R^n (Heine–Borel). Example: closed intervals in R are bounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact subset (metric space)
rubrics_metrics.description: K ⊂ X is compact if every open cover of K has a finite subcover of K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: any finite set is compact. Use open-cover criterion to prove other properties (e.g., closedness, boundedness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: K ⊂ X is sequentially compact if every sequence of points in K has a convergent subsequence converging to a point in K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the subsequence formulation of compactness used frequently in metric-space arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: compact iff sequentially compact (metric spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any metric space (X,d), a subset K is compact if and only if it is sequentially compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits into: (1) compact ⇒ sequentially compact by finite subcover argument producing a constant subsequence; (2) sequentially compact ⇒ compact by constructing a sequence outside finite unions when no finite subcover exists and reaching contradiction via subsequence convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact sets are closed and bounded (in metric spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is (sequentially) compact in a metric space (X,d), then K is closed and bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closedness: show complement is open using sequences; boundedness: if not bounded produce sequence with distances > n and extract convergent subsequence to get contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subset of compact set is compact
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is compact and S is closed with S ⊂ K, then S is compact (equivalently, K ∩ S is compact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given open cover of S, add complement of S to get open cover of K; finite subcover of K yields finite cover of S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite intersection property for compact sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For a collection {K_α | α∈Λ} of compact subsets of X, the intersection of every finite subcollection is nonempty iff ⋂_{α∈Λ} K_α is nonempty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: use complements to convert to open cover of one K_α and apply compactness to deduce contradiction if full intersection empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nested compact sets intersection nonempty
rubrics_metrics.description: If {K_n} is a sequence of nonempty compact subsets with K_{n+1} ⊂ K_n for n≥1, then ⋂_{n≥1} K_n ≠ ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary of finite intersection property (or compactness and decreasing sequence argument). Examples contrasting open vs closed nested intervals are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heine–Borel theorem (R^n special case)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset K ⊂ R is (sequentially) compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine general metric-space results (compact ⇒ closed & bounded) with compactness of closed intervals in R via interval-halving proof (Proposition 3.17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass theorem (bounded sequences have convergent subsequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each bounded sequence in R has a convergent subsequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Heine–Borel: bounded sequence lies in closed interval which is sequentially compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sequence and subsequence in R
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence {x_n} is a map from Z_+ to R. A subsequence is indexed via an increasing injective map s: Z_+ → Z_+, written {x_{n_k}} with n_k = s(k) and n_1 < n_2 < ⋯.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subsequences to analyze cluster points, lim sup/lim inf, and to extract convergent subsequences from bounded sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon-N definition of convergence (sequences in R)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence {x_n} converges to x0 if for every ε>0 there exists N such that whenever n>N, |x_n − x0| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation: lim_{n→∞} x_n = x0 or x_n → x0. Equivalent characterizations include: every open disk around x0 contains all but finitely many terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of convergent sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniqueness of limits; equivalence with open-disk containment; every subsequence converges to the same limit; convergent sequences are bounded; set of subsequential limits is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard facts to check when manipulating limits and subsequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Squeeze (sandwich) theorem for sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n ≤ y_n ≤ z_n eventually and x_n → a, z_n → a, then y_n → a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the pointwise inequalities and the fact max{|x_n−a|,|z_n−a|}→0 to bound |y_n−a|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra of limits (sum, product, quotient)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n→x and y_n→y then x_n±y_n→x±y; x_n y_n→xy; and x_n / y_n → x / y provided y_n≠0 and y≠0 (with appropriate bounds used in proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use triangular inequality and boundedness of sequences to prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence to ±∞ (sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: x_n → +∞ means for any M>0 there exists N with n>N ⇒ x_n > M. Similarly for −∞. Such sequences are divergent in R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotone comparisons preserve divergence: if x_n ≤ y_n and x_n → +∞ then y_n → +∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy sequence (metric spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence {x_n} is Cauchy if for every ε>0 there exists N such that for m,n > N, d(x_m,x_n) < ε (equivalently d(x_{n+p},x_n)<ε for all p≥0 eventually).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergent ⇒ Cauchy in any metric space; in R the converse holds (completeness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of Cauchy sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Range of a Cauchy sequence is bounded. If a Cauchy sequence has a convergent subsequence then the whole sequence converges to the same limit. In a compact subset, every Cauchy sequence converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ε=1 to get boundedness; use triangle inequality and subsequence convergence to deduce full convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of R (Cauchy ⇔ convergent)
rubrics_metrics.description: In R, a sequence is convergent iff it is a Cauchy sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses that any Cauchy sequence is bounded, so lies in a closed interval which is compact; hence sequential compactness yields a convergent subsequence and Proposition 1.16 implies convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: lim sup and lim inf (subsequential limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: For {x_n}, let L be set of all subsequential limits (include ±∞ if some subsequence diverges). Define lim sup x_n = sup L (possibly +∞) and lim inf x_n = inf L (possibly −∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence converges to a iff lim sup = lim inf = a. Various monotonic tail properties: if x > sup L then eventually x_n < x, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series and partial sums (definition of series convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given terms x_n, partial sums s_n = Σ_{k=1}^n x_k. The infinite series Σ x_n converges if s_n has a finite limit as n→∞ (otherwise diverges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recover x_n from s_n by differences; many convergence tests operate on partial sums or tails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's criterion for series
rubrics_metrics.description: Series Σ x_n converges iff for every ε>0 there exists N such that for all n>N and p≥0, |Σ_{k=n}^{n+p} x_k| < ε (i.e., tails can be made arbitrarily small).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollary: if Σ x_n converges then x_n → 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating-series (Leibniz) test
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n ≥ x_{n+1} ≥ 0 for all n and x_n → 0, then Σ (-1)^n x_n converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Cauchy's criterion: alternating tail sums are bounded by the first omitted term which → 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonnegative-term series monotone test
rubrics_metrics.description: For a series with nonnegative terms, it converges iff its sequence of partial sums is bounded (since partial sums are monotone nondecreasing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for p-series and comparison tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute convergence implies convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ |x_n| converges, then Σ x_n converges (absolutely ⇒ convergent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via Cauchy criterion and comparison: |Σ tail x_k| ≤ Σ tail |x_k|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison test (direct comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) If |x_n| ≤ y_n for all n and Σ y_n converges, then Σ x_n converges absolutely. (2) If x_n ≤ y_n for all n and Σ x_n = +∞, then Σ y_n = +∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to show convergence/divergence of series by bounding with known series (e.g., p-series).

rubrics_metrics.name: p-series criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The series Σ 1/n^p converges iff p > 1; if p ≤ 1 it diverges to +∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via dyadic grouping lemma (Lemma 2.10) reducing to a geometric series; special case: harmonic series (p=1) diverges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root test
rubrics_metrics.description: For series Σ x_n define α = lim sup_{n→∞} (|x_n|)^{1/n}. If α < 1 the series converges absolutely; if α > 1 it diverges; α = 1 inconclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparison with geometric series |x_n| < β^n for some β∈(α,1) when α<1; example showing α=1 inconclusive: p-series produce α=1 with varying outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio test
rubrics_metrics.description: For series Σ x_n define α = lim sup |x_{n+1}/x_n|. If α < 1 the series converges absolutely. If eventually |x_{n+1}/x_n| ≥ 1 (or lim inf > 1) then the series diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiplicative comparison |x_{n+k}| ≤ |x_n| β^k to compare with geometric series when α<1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radius of convergence for power series
rubrics_metrics.description: For power series Σ c_n x^n set α = lim sup (|c_n|)^{1/n}. Then radius R = 1/α (with α=0 ⇒ R=+∞, α=+∞ ⇒ R=0). The series converges for |x|<R and diverges for |x|>R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard root-test consequence for power series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of e and limit (1+1/n)^n
rubrics_metrics.description: Define e = Σ_{k=0}^∞ 1/k!. The sequence (1 + 1/n)^n converges to e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use binomial expansion to compare (1+1/n)^n to partial sums of e and squeeze between sequences converging to e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication (Cauchy product) of series and Mertens' theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Given Σ a_n = A and Σ b_n = B, define c_n = Σ_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n−k} (Cauchy product). If Σ a_n converges absolutely (and Σ b_n converges), then Σ c_n converges to A·B (Mertens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute partial sums and estimate using absolute convergence of one factor; note product series may diverge if absolute convergence fails (counterexample provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abel's result on multiplication of series
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ a_n = A, Σ b_n = B and Σ c_n = C where c_n = Σ_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n−k}, then C = A·B (Abel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abel's theorem relates convolution of coefficients to product of sums; proof uses continuity properties of power series (deferred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ x_n is conditionally convergent (convergent but not absolutely), then by Riemann’s theorem its terms can be rearranged so that partial sums have prescribed lim inf and lim sup (in particular can be rearranged to converge to any real number or to diverge). Conversely, if Σ x_n is absolutely convergent then every rearrangement converges absolutely to the same limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates the crucial difference between absolute and conditional convergence; be careful when rearranging non-absolutely convergent series.
